title: First calumny answered: remitted-sins persuasion is not Reformed formal act of faith
source_text: CXXXI. Sed jam breviter singula perstringamus. Atque ut ea ordine retrogrado resumam, incipiendo a posterioribus; Annon clarum est, ex iis quae fuse supra deduximus, Per calumniam Theologis Reformatis tribui, quod communi consensu doceant proprium & formalem fidei actum, per quem justificamur, esse certam persuasionem quae singulis fidelibus inest, quod peccata ipsis remissa sunt, & quod sunt coram Deo justi: adeoque talem persuasionem ita necessariam esse, ut absque ea nemo vere fidelis & justus esse possit, non secus ac si credere detrectaret aliquem ex praecipuis & fundamentalibus fidei articulis? Nam saepius jam allata sunt testimonia Perkinsii, Davenantii, Amesii, Mestrezatii, Petri Molinaei, Antonii Walaei, & Wittichii, qui in eo sequitur Widmarium, qui expresse negant fiduciam, quae est fidei salvificae actus formalis atque praecipuus, eam esse qua certi & persuasi sumus de gratia jam impetrata; sed eam per quam ad Deum confugimus eique innitimur, ut misericordiam per Christum consequamur: & priorem illam fiduciam posse a vere fideli & justificato abesse, & saltem ad tempus a fide separari: quae est etiam aperta doctrina Confessionis Anglicanae, a Theologis Presbyterianis conscriptae atque publicatae. Num igitur citra calumniam dici possunt communi consensu docere Reformati, quod negant tot inter eos Theologiae Professores scriptis suis celebrati, imo illae ipsae, quibus plurimi eorum subscribunt, fidei Confessiones? Ut omittam eos qui quaestionem illam expresse non moventes, alia tamen in re formam & essentiam fidei constituunt quam in illa persuasione de obtenta jam a Deo remissione peccatorum, ut Musculum & Petrum Martyrem, quibus fides est simpliciter firmus & constans assensus cordis ad ea quae vel narrantur, vel promittuntur Verbo, a Spiritu Sancto afflatus ad salutem credentium: quique firmum assensum exponunt, per eum qui sit tantarum virium & efficaciae, ut secum trahat affectum fiduciae, spei & charitatis, & omnia tandem bona opera; & similiter credere in Deum, qui ipsis est praecipuus actus fidei salvificae, exponunt per spem omnem in Deum dirigere, firmaque fiducia ab illius bonitate pendere.
pass_a_gloss: But now briefly let us touch each point. And that I may resume them in reverse order, beginning from the later ones: Is it not clear, from those things which we have drawn out at length above, that it is attributed by calumny to the Reformed Theologians that by common consent they teach the proper and formal act of faith through which we are justified to be the certain persuasion which is in each of the faithful, that their sins are remitted to them, and that they are just before God — and moreover that such persuasion is so necessary that without it no one can be truly faithful and just, no otherwise than if he refused to believe some one of the chief and fundamental articles of faith? For often already have been brought forward the testimonies of Perkins, Davenant, Ames, Mestrezat, Pierre Du Moulin, Antonius Walaeus, and Wittich, who in that follows Widmar, who expressly deny that the fiducia which is the formal and chief act of saving faith is that by which we are certain and persuaded concerning grace already obtained; but rather that by which we flee to God and lean upon him, that we may obtain mercy through Christ: and that the former fiducia can be absent from one truly faithful and justified, and at least for a time be separated from faith — which is also the open doctrine of the Anglican Confession, written and published by the Presbyterian Theologians. Can the Reformed therefore without calumny be said to teach by common consent what so many among them celebrated Professors of Theology by their writings deny — nay, those very Confessions of faith to which many of them subscribe? Not to mention those who, though not expressly moving that question, nevertheless constitute the form and essence of faith in something other than that persuasion concerning remission of sins already obtained from God — as Musculus and Peter Martyr, for whom faith is simply the firm and constant assent of the heart to those things which are either narrated or promised by the Word, breathed by the Holy Spirit unto the salvation of believers: and who explain firm assent as that which is of such strength and efficacy that it draws with itself the affection of fiducia, hope, and charity, and at length all good works; and likewise explain believing in God, which for them is the chief act of saving faith, as directing all hope toward God and depending with firm fiducia upon his goodness.
pass_b_english: Briefly, taking the charges in reverse: it is calumny to say Reformed theologians teach by common consent that faith's formal justifying act is each believer's certain persuasion that sins are remitted and he is just before God — and that without that persuasion none is truly faithful, as if denying a fundamental article.

Perkins, Davenant, Ames, Mestrezat, Du Moulin, Walaeus, and Wittich following Widmar expressly deny that saving faith's formal act is already-obtained-grace certainty; it is rather fleeing to God and leaning on him for mercy through Christ — and the former trust can be absent even from the justified for a time, as also the Presbyterian Anglican Confession teaches.
Musculus and Peter Martyr likewise place faith's essence in Spirit-wrought firm heart-assent that draws fiducia, hope, charity, and good works — not in remitted-sins persuasion.
